message.content:
The number of distinct positions that can arise in a game of chess is astronomically large.  In fact, the best estimates put it at roughly **10^43** (between 10^43 and 10^50).  

This figure is often called the *Shannon number* after Claude Shannon, who first estimated it in 1950.  It represents the size of the game‑tree complexity of chess – the number of different legal board configurations that can occur during a game, taking into account all the rules (piece types, colors, castling rights, en‑passant possibilities, etc.).  

If you ignore the rules and just count how many ways you could place the 32 pieces (16 white, 16 black) on the 64 squares, you get a much larger number (on the order of 10^52), but that includes illegal positions (e.g., two kings in check, pawns on the 8th rank, etc.).  The 10^43 figure is the accepted estimate for the number of *legal* positions.
